excerpt: Paano magtanim ng upo? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant upo (bottle gourd), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant upo. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino farmers grow upo on an overhead trellis, from sprouted seed in hills to young fruits cut about two weeks after they set. It is for small farms and backyards that sell or cook the young fruits and tops.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for cucurbits](/land-preparation/cucurbit-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [upo varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/upo). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [upo nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/bottle-gourd-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng gulay](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-gulay), [vegetables in the Philippines](/crops/vegetables-philippines).
When to plant upo

Upo grows in both the wet and dry seasons but does best in warm, fairly dry weather. Wet season plantings go on ridges or raised beds with good drainage, since the vines dislike soggy soil, and dry season plantings need weekly irrigation.
What you plant

Seed, about 1 to 3 kg for a hectare. Farmers soak the seed in clean water overnight or up to a day, wrap it in a damp cloth in a cool, dark corner until the shell cracks open, and plant it straight in the hills. Hybrid seed is often raised in trays and transplanted about 15 days after it comes up.
Paano magtanim ng upo, step by step

Fruits reach market size about 15 days after they set, which is about 60 to 80 days after sowing depending on the variety. Picking then goes on every few days. The crop is ready about 65 days after sowing.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 21 days before sowing: Plow and harrow the field
items.text: Plow 15 to 20 cm deep two or three times, a week apart, so weeds sprout and get turned under each time. Harrow after each plowing to break the clods.

items.title: 2 days before sowing: Open the furrows
items.text: Make furrows 2 to 3 meters apart. In the wet season plant on the ridges or on raised beds and dig canals so water drains away.

items.title: 1 day before sowing: Soak and sprout the seed
items.text: Soak the seed overnight in clean water, then wrap it in a damp cloth and keep it in a cool, dark place until the seed coat splits.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Sowing day: Fertilize and plant the hills
items.text: Put well rotted manure and about 20 grams of 14 14 14 in each hill and cover it with a little soil so it does not touch the seed. Plant one or two sprouted seeds a hill, about 1 meter apart along the furrow, and cover thinly.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 5: Replant missing hills
items.text: Replant hills where nothing came up within the first week.

items.title: Day 7: Water weekly and mulch
items.text: In the dry season irrigate the furrows about once a week. Lay a ring of rice straw at the foot of each plant so the soil stays damp and you water less.

items.title: Day 10: Build the overhead trellis
items.text: Build a flat roof about 2 meters high over rows 2 to 3 meters wide, on ipil ipil or bamboo posts, with tie wire or nylon twine woven across and along the top. Give each plant a pole or a string ladder to climb. Tip: In the wet season the trellis keeps the fruits off the ground, where they rot and grow crooked.

items.title: Day 18: Hill up
items.text: Between 15 and 20 days after the seedlings come up, push soil against the base of the plants and pull the weeds.

items.title: Day 20: Train and prune the vines
items.text: Tie the stem loosely to its pole until it reaches the roof. Remove side branches and female buds on the main stem below the roof, then cut the vine tip once it reaches the top so fruiting branches spread out.

items.title: Day 30: First side dressing
items.text: About 30 days after planting, put about 10 grams of urea at each hill, some 10 cm from the stem so it does not burn the plant, and cover it.

items.title: Day 35: Watch for beetles and fruit rot
items.text: Pick and crush the yellow leaf beetles, and some farmers dust wood ash on the leaves to keep them off. Collect and remove rotting fruits and keep the field clean. Tip: Upo flowers open in the late afternoon, so never spray then. The insects that pollinate the flowers come at the same time.

items.title: Day 40: Hand weed only
items.text: Once the vines bear, stop hoeing or plowing between rows so the spreading roots are not cut. Pull weeds by hand.

items.title: Day 45: Second side dressing
items.text: About 45 days after planting, give each hill about 20 grams of urea and 10 grams of muriate of potash, away from the stem, and cover it.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 65: Cut the young fruits
items.text: Upo fruits grow fast, so walk the trellis every day or two. Cut fruits that have reached market size, about 15 days after they set, with a sharp knife, leaving about 5 cm of stalk.

items.title: Day 66: Pack without bruising
items.text: Line a bamboo basket with banana leaves and lay the fruits in it, then pack the good ones in plastic bags or crates for market.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for upo
Spacing
Furrows 2 to 3 meters apart and hills about 1 meter apart along the row, one or two plants a hill.
Water

Upo dislikes soggy soil, which brings disease, so wet season fields need drainage canals and ridges. In the dry season the furrows are irrigated about once a week, and a ring of rice straw at the foot of each plant keeps the soil damp longer.
Fertilizer

Well rotted manure and about 20 grams of 14 14 14 a hill at planting, covered with soil. About 10 grams of urea a hill at 30 days, and about 20 grams of urea with 10 grams of muriate of potash a hill at 45 days, placed some 10 cm from the stem. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

An overhead trellis about 2 meters high on ipil ipil or bamboo, with a pole or string for each plant. Vines are tied as they climb, the shoots and female buds below the roof are removed, and the vine tip is cut at the roof. Hilling up at 15 to 20 days, then only hand weeding once the vines bear. Yellow beetles are picked by hand, and some farmers dust wood ash on the leaves.
When and how to harvest

Fruits are cut about 15 days after they set, 60 to 80 days after sowing, with a sharp knife leaving about 5 cm of stalk. Because they grow fast the trellis is checked every day or two. Fruits are laid in bamboo baskets with banana leaves at the bottom, then packed in plastic bags or crates. Fully mature fruits with a hard rind are kept for seed or dried for containers and crafts.
Common mistakes when planting upo

items: Planting on flat, wet ground in the rainy months, which brings fruit rot and dying vines.
Spraying in the late afternoon, which kills the insects that pollinate the flowers.
Hoeing between rows while the vines bear, which cuts the spreading roots.
Letting fruits grow past market size, so they turn hard and do not sell.
Putting fertilizer right against the stem, which burns the young plant.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of upo
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Have the soil tested and feed by the result, with potash in the fruiting weeks.
Choose a variety that sets fruit well in your season and that buyers in your market like.
Hand pollinate in the late afternoon when few insects visit, to get more fruits set.
Use yellow sticky traps and hand picking for leaf beetles, and remove rotting fruits every day.
Rotate away from other gourds and melons so pests and soil diseases do not build up.
Mulch every row with rice straw or plastic to save water and weeding.
